issues.legal_issue: Eyewitness identification and supporting evidence can sustain a murder conviction despite challenges based on darkness, witness relationship, stomach contents, and the absence of blood on a weapon when the circumstances explain those matters and the evidence is corroborated.
material_facts: The incident occurred at night in an open field on a cloudless, starry night, and the witnesses knew the accused.
One eyewitness was close to the accused and physically struggled with one of them; another witness arrived at the scene and corroborated the first witness’s account of the accused’s presence.
The medical evidence found a few undigested rice particles in the deceased’s stomach, but such particles may remain after the usual digestion period.
The accused’s knife had no detected blood stain; the injury attributed to him was superficial, and he had thrown the knife.
issues.conclusion: The evidentiary objections did not create a serious doubt about the prosecution case, and the conviction was supported by reliable evidence.
issues.legal_principle: Identification of known persons at close range may be possible in a cloudless, starry night in an open place. Undigested food after the usual digestion period is not, by itself, decisive evidence of the time of death; Modi’s Medical Jurisprudence and Toxicology is cited on variation in digestion. The absence of blood on a weapon is not decisive where the injury was superficial and the circumstances reasonably explain the absence of a stain.

rule.if: murder_conviction_appeal and known_assailants and identification_conditions_permitted_observation and eyewitness_account_was_corroborated and medical_timing_evidence_was_not_decisive and absence_of_weapon_blood_was_explained

predicates.murder_conviction_appeal: The proceeding was an appeal challenging a murder conviction entered after an acquittal was reversed.
predicates.known_assailants: The eyewitnesses knew the persons they identified as the assailants.
predicates.identification_conditions_permitted_obse: The incident occurred in an open place on a cloudless, starry night, and an eyewitness observed an assailant at close range while struggling with him.
predicates.eyewitness_account_was_corroborated: A second witness corroborated the first witness’s account of the accused’s presence at the scene.
predicates.medical_timing_evidence_was_not_decisive: The medical examination found a few undigested rice particles, and the evidence allowed for digestion to take longer than usual.
predicates.absence_of_weapon_blood_was_explained: The weapon had no blood stain, the injury attributed to its user was superficial, and the user threw the weapon.

issues.definition: When a murder conviction is appealed and the identified assailants were known, observation was possible, the eyewitness account was corroborated, and the medical and weapon evidence did not decisively contradict it, the conviction may be sustained as supported by reliable evidence.

issues.legal_issue: Common intention to commit a homicide may be inferred from the participants’ coordinated conduct, and an independently proved overt act by each participant is not a legal requirement for shared liability for the homicide.
material_facts: The accused went together, armed with knives, concealed themselves, and waited for the deceased.
When the deceased arrived, the accused emerged and announced that they had been waiting for him.
One accused began the attack and was prevented by a witness from continuing; the other pursued and inflicted the fatal injuries.
The accused whose attack was interrupted was convicted of the homicide together with the other participant.
issues.conclusion: The evidence permitted the inference that the accused shared the intention to kill, and the conviction for the homicide with the aid of common intention was justified even if he had not caused the head injury.
issues.legal_principle: Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code applies when a criminal act is done by several persons in furtherance of their common intention; proof of an overt act by every participant is not a requirement. Common intention may be inferred from the proved circumstances. The Court relied on Chinta Pulla Reddy v. State of Andhra Pradesh, [1993] Supp. (3) SCC 134, where a participant’s conviction under Section 302 read with Section 34 was upheld although another accused alone inflicted the fatal injuries.

rule.if: joint_homicide_prosecution and participants_concealed_themselves_together and participants_were_armed_and_waiting_for_the_victim and participants_announced_their_joint_wait and one_participant_initiated_the_attack and another_participant_inflicted_fatal_injuries

predicates.joint_homicide_prosecution: The proceeding concerned whether a participant in a homicide was liable for the act committed by another participant.
predicates.participants_concealed_themselves_togeth: The participants concealed themselves together before the victim arrived.
predicates.participants_were_armed_and_waiting_for_: The participants were armed and waited together for the victim.
predicates.participants_announced_their_joint_wait: The participants announced to the victim that they had been waiting for him.
predicates.one_participant_initiated_the_attack: One participant began attacking the victim and was prevented from continuing by another person.
predicates.another_participant_inflicted_fatal_inju: Another participant inflicted the injuries that caused the victim’s death.

issues.definition: When participants jointly conceal themselves, wait armed for a victim, announce their joint purpose, and take part in an attack in which one inflicts the fatal injuries, a participant may share liability for the homicide without proof that each inflicted an injury.
